title: Agile and Scrum Essentials
summary: Learn agile ways of working: the Agile Manifesto, Scrum roles, events and artifacts, user stories and backlogs, story points, velocity and forecasting, Kanban and flow, and effective retrospectives.
audience: Project team members, developers, product managers, students and anyone working in fast-changing projects

body.p: Agile is an approach to work in which teams deliver value in small pieces, get feedback quickly and adapt plans as they learn. It began in software, where long fixed plans often produced products nobody wanted by the time they were finished, and is now used in marketing, product design, banking, government and education.

list: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
Working results over comprehensive documentation.
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
Responding to change over following a plan.

body.p: The items on the right still matter; agile teams simply value those on the left more. Agile is not "no planning": it is frequent, lighter planning, guided by what each delivery teaches.

Waterfall projects move through fixed stages (requirements, design, build, test, release) and deliver at the end. That suits work with stable, well-understood requirements, such as some construction. Agile suits uncertain work, where users only know what they want after trying something.

body.tip: Ask, "What is the smallest useful thing we could deliver in two weeks?" That question captures the agile mindset.

body.p: Scrum is the most widely used agile framework. Work happens in sprints: fixed periods of one to four weeks, often two, each producing a usable increment.

list: Product owner: maximises value, owns and orders the product backlog, and decides what is most important.
Scrum master: coaches the team and organisation in Scrum, removes obstacles and protects the process.
Developers: everyone who builds the increment, whatever their specialism; the team organises its own work.
Sprint planning: choose the sprint goal and the backlog items to deliver.
Daily scrum: a 15-minute check on progress towards the sprint goal and any blockers.
Sprint review: show the increment to stakeholders and gather feedback.
Sprint retrospective: improve how the team works.
Product backlog: an ordered list of everything that might be built.
Sprint backlog: the items chosen for this sprint plus the plan to deliver them.
Increment: the working result, meeting the team's definition of done.

body.tip: Keep the daily scrum focused on the sprint goal; detailed problem-solving happens afterwards with only the people needed.

body.p: Backlog items are often written as user stories: short descriptions of value from a user's point of view: "As a market trader, I want to record a sale in two taps so that I can serve the next customer quickly."

list: Independent where possible, so they can be built in any order.
Negotiable: details are worked out in conversation.
Valuable to a user or customer.
Estimable and small enough to finish within a sprint.
Testable, with clear acceptance criteria, for example: "Given I am offline, when I record a sale, then it syncs once I reconnect."

body.p: Large items (epics) are split into smaller stories: by user type, by step in a workflow, or by simple-then-advanced versions. The product owner keeps the top of the backlog small, clear and ready, while lower items can stay rough.

body.tip: If a story cannot be shown working to a user at the sprint review, it is probably a task, not a story.

body.p: Many teams estimate relative effort in story points instead of hours, often using a Fibonacci-like scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) because bigger items are harder to estimate precisely. Planning poker, where everyone reveals an estimate at once, avoids being anchored by the loudest voice.

Velocity is the number of points a team completes per sprint. If the last three sprints delivered 21, 24 and 27 points, the average velocity is 72 / 3 = 24. With 120 points left in the backlog, the forecast is 120 / 24 = 5 sprints, or 10 weeks with two-week sprints. Forecasts improve as you learn; give ranges, not promises.
A burndown chart shows work remaining against time. If a sprint started with 40 points and 28 are done, 12 remain. A flat line warns early that the sprint goal is at risk.

list: Velocity is for the team's planning, not for comparing teams or judging people.
Points only count when work meets the definition of done.

body.tip: When a forecast looks bad, cut scope by moving lower-value items down the backlog rather than asking the team to work longer hours.

body.p: Kanban is another agile method, focused on continuous flow rather than sprints. Work items move across a board with columns such as To do, In progress, Review and Done.

list: Visualise all work on the board, including urgent requests.
Limit work in progress (WIP): for example, no more than three items In progress. Finishing beats starting.
Measure flow: cycle time (how long one item takes) and throughput (items finished per day or week).
Make policies explicit, such as what "done" means for each column.
Improve continuously based on the data.

body.p: Average cycle time = average work in progress / average throughput. If a team has 12 items in progress and finishes 3 a day, items take about 12 / 3 = 4 days. Cutting WIP to 6 at the same throughput halves the average cycle time to 2 days.

body.tip: If everyone is busy but little is finished, too much work has been started; lower the WIP limit.

body.p: Continuous improvement is the heart of agile. In a retrospective, the team asks what went well, what did not, and what one or two changes to try next sprint. Changes are small experiments, reviewed at the next retrospective.

list: Make it safe: focus on systems and processes, not blaming individuals.
Use data, such as the burndown chart and incidents.
Agree a few concrete actions with owners, not a long wish list.
Check whether last time's actions helped.
Doing the ceremonies without the mindset ("agile in name only").
A product owner without real authority, or one unavailable to the team.
Sprints overloaded from the start, so goals are always missed.
Skipping testing to meet sprint deadlines, which builds up hidden defects.
Using velocity as a performance target, which leads to inflated estimates.

body.p: Large organisations coordinate many teams with frameworks such as Scrum of Scrums, LeSS or SAFe, but the basics still matter most: small batches, clear priorities, quality and fast feedback.

body.tip: Pick one improvement per retrospective and actually finish it; small consistent changes add up.

options: Responding to change over following a plan
